description: Here at Galactic Genius, we are engineers, artists, and just high school nerds who love computer science.
summary: GO / NO-GO is an interactive spacecraft mission-design and mission-operations simulator that helps learners explore how engineering decisions shape the success of a space mission. Users select a mission scenario, assemble a spacecraft architecture, configure subsystems and payloads, choose an orbit and launch configuration, and review engineering checks covering mass, power, propulsion, thermal behaviour, communications, storage and mission risks. They can address findings, make the final launch decision, run a mission simulation and review a scored debrief. The experience supports Earth, lunar, Mars and asteroid mission contexts, with planetary visualisation and supporting Earth-observation capabilities. The project combines a browser-based 3D environment with engineering calculations and mission workflow tools, while NASA's GIBS imagery services and NASA's Mission-Viz resources support its Earth-observation and space-visualisation context. GO / NO-GO aims to make systems engineering more understandable, interactive and approachable by letting users learn through designing, testing and operating missions—not just reading about them.
details:
What the project does

GO / NO-GO is a browser-based spacecraft mission-design, engineering-verification and mission-operations simulator. It gives users a structured way to develop a space mission from an initial concept through spacecraft configuration, orbital planning, engineering review, launch and mission debrief. The project is designed to make the relationships between mission objectives and engineering trade-offs visible and interactive.

How it works

A user begins by choosing a mission scenario, such as a lunar scout, Mars observer or asteroid explorer. The user then develops a spacecraft architecture by selecting a bus and configuring supported subsystems and mission equipment. The design process covers payload capability, mass, electrical power, energy storage, propulsion, thermal control, avionics, communications and data storage. The user selects an appropriate orbit and launch configuration, then defines or reviews the mission profile and operational constraints.

Before launch, the engineering-verification stage evaluates the design using the simulator's engineering calculations and compatibility checks. Findings are presented as actionable issues rather than only a pass/fail indicator. The user can review resource margins, understand the likely consequences of a problem, revise the design and make the final launch decision. The application retains the distinction between the system's GO / CAUTION / NO-GO recommendation and the user's launch authorisation. The mission simulation then produces operational results and a debrief with a weighted score across science value, reliability and mission completion, resource efficiency, data and communications, and risk management.

Engineering and learning value

The simulator brings several connected engineering disciplines into one workflow. Its calculations and checks address mass budgets, power generation and consumption, battery depth of discharge, propulsion and delta-v, orbital mechanics, thermal balance, radio-frequency link budgets, storage and downlink capacity, and mission reliability. Findings help users see why a spacecraft can be suitable in one mission context but unsuitable in another. The intention is to reward sound engineering decisions and mission-objective fit, rather than a particular spacecraft brand, component combination or orbit.

The project supports Earth, Moon, Mars and asteroid mission contexts. It uses planetary visualisation to make mission environments and orbital relationships easier to understand. NASA's Global Imagery Browse Services (GIBS) provide NASA Earth-observation visualisations for supporting Earth-context features. NASA's open-source Web-based Space Mission Visualization (Mission-Viz) project is included among the project's resources and provides relevant examples and reference material for orbital and mission visualisation. These resources complement the simulator; GO / NO-GO is an independent educational project and is not an official NASA product or certification system.

Benefits and intended impact

GO / NO-GO is intended for students, educators, space enthusiasts and emerging engineers who want to understand how space missions are designed and evaluated. Instead of presenting spacecraft as fixed, idealised products, it lets users test alternative architectures, encounter engineering constraints and observe the consequences of their decisions. This can make multidisciplinary systems engineering more accessible, encourage critical thinking and help learners connect scientific goals to real engineering trade-offs. The debrief and leaderboard add a repeatable challenge that encourages users to improve their designs and compare mission outcomes.

Tools and technologies

The application is built as a web experience using React, TypeScript and Vite. Three.js and React Three Fiber support interactive 3D scenes and planetary/spacecraft visualisation. Zustand is used for application state. Supabase supports the international leaderboard and related backend data workflows. Cloudflare Pages and Pages Functions are used for hosting and server-side functionality. The project also uses NASA GIBS for Earth-observation visualisations and includes NASA Mission-Viz resources. Microsoft Planetary Computer's STAC services and Meteomatics are supporting third-party geospatial/weather services; they are not NASA-operated resources.

Creative approach and design considerations

The central creative idea is to combine a spacecraft-building experience with an engineering review and mission simulation. The user is not limited to choosing a preselected “correct” spacecraft. Instead, the application encourages experimentation while checking whether the resulting design is compatible with its mission. The project considers mission-specific environments, subsystem dependencies, resource margins, technical uncertainty and the need to explain engineering findings clearly. It distinguishes physical laws, engineering approximations and simulator/gameplay rules so users can better understand the basis of a result.
